stem: Based on the texts, both authors would most likely agree with which statement?
stimulus:
Text 1
In a study of mouse lymph nodes, immunologist Rhea Okonjo's team counted germinal centers, the clusters where B cells refine the antibodies they produce. They found roughly half as many in aged mice as in young ones. Because B cells drive germinal-center formation, the team concluded that B cells lose this capacity with age.

Text 2
Using higher-resolution imaging, Tomas Lindqvist confirmed Okonjo's count. His images also showed that aged nodes contain far fewer follicular dendritic cells, which display the antigens B cells must encounter before forming germinal centers. A shortage of these cells could by itself limit germinal centers, Lindqvist notes, even if aged B cells remain fully capable.
choices: The lymph nodes of aged mice hold fewer of the sites where B cells refine antibodies than those of young mice do.
B cells in aged mice are less able than B cells in young mice to start forming new germinal centers.
A shortage of follicular dendritic cells is the main reason that germinal centers decline in aged mice.
Imaging at lower resolution probably overstated how few germinal centers the aged mice actually had.
explanation: Split Text 1 into its observation and its inference. The observation is that aged mice have about half as many germinal centers. The inference is that aged B cells lose the ability to form them. Lindqvist 'confirmed Okonjo's count', so he accepts the observation and challenges only the inference by naming another possible cause: too few follicular dendritic cells. The one thing both authors hold is the observation. Choice A restates it, using Text 1's definition of germinal centers as the clusters where B cells refine antibodies.

B.why: This is Okonjo's inference, not something both authors accept. Lindqvist says aged B cells may 'remain fully capable', and that is exactly the conclusion he is questioning. You picked the claim Text 1 ends on without checking whether Text 2 accepts it.

C.why: You saw that Text 2 offers another cause and then made it stronger than it is. Lindqvist only says the shortage 'could' limit germinal centers, so he doesn't call it the main reason. Okonjo blames the B cells, so she wouldn't agree with this either.

D.why: This is the trap for this subtype: you treated Text 2 as an attack on the data. The higher-resolution imaging confirmed the count instead of correcting it. Lindqvist disputes what the count means, not the count itself.

stem: Based on the texts, both authors would most likely agree with which statement?
stimulus:
Text 1
When engineer Priya Haddad repeatedly loaded 3D-printed titanium brackets, they cracked after far fewer cycles than forged brackets did. Microscopy showed a small pore at the origin of nearly every crack. Haddad therefore concluded that porosity left by printing is what shortens the brackets' fatigue lives.

Text 2
Re-examining Haddad's brackets with high-resolution x-ray tomography, Felipe Arce did find pores at the crack origins. Yet those pores sit where unusually coarse grains meet, and such boundaries concentrate stress on their own. It is difficult to exclude, Arce argues, that the grain boundaries start the cracks and the pores simply happen to lie nearby.
choices: In the printed brackets, fatigue cracks tended to begin at locations where pores were present.
The pores left by printing are what cause the printed brackets to crack after fewer cycles.
Coarse grain boundaries, not pores, are what cause the printed brackets to crack early.
Ordinary microscopy mistook features at the crack origins for pores that were not really there.
explanation: Text 1's observation is that a pore sat at the origin of nearly every crack. Its inference, marked by 'therefore', is that porosity causes the early failure. Arce's tomography 'did find pores at the crack origins', so he accepts the observation. He then names another possible source of the same pattern: coarse grain boundaries that concentrate stress, with the pores 'simply' nearby. Both authors therefore agree only that cracks began where pores were, which is choice A.

B.why: This is Haddad's 'therefore' conclusion, and it is the claim Text 2 was written to challenge. Arce suggests the pores may just be nearby while the grain boundaries start the cracks, so he wouldn't agree with it.

C.why: You spotted Arce's alternative cause and then stated it as settled fact. He says only that it is 'difficult to exclude', which raises a possibility without proving it. Haddad blames the pores, so she would reject this choice as well.

D.why: This is the subtype trap: you read the new imaging method as overturning the old data. Arce's tomography confirmed that the pores were really there. He questions what they mean, not whether they exist.

stem: Based on the texts, both authors would most likely agree with which statement?
stimulus:
Text 1
Comparing charts produced by a single Venetian workshop, historian Livia Morandi found that coastlines on its charts from after 1583 match modern surveys far more closely than those on its earlier charts. Because the improvement is abrupt rather than gradual, Morandi concluded that the workshop had begun receiving measurements taken by pilots on newly commissioned voyages.

Text 2
Morandi is right that the later charts are more accurate. But multispectral imaging reveals that their coastlines were redrawn over erased earlier outlines, and the new outlines match, inlet for inlet, those of a Genoese chart the workshop acquired in 1583. An abrupt gain in accuracy could simply reflect copying a rival's work.
choices: The workshop's later coastlines were drawn from measurements its own pilots took at sea.
The workshop's later charts drew on information that it did not have before 1583.
The later charts seem more accurate only because their coastlines were redrawn.
The erased outlines under the later coastlines record the workshop's earlier survey methods.
explanation: Split Text 1 into its observation (the charts made after 1583 are abruptly more accurate) and its inference (pilots' new measurements caused this). Text 2 accepts the observation and offers a different source: a rival chart acquired in 1583. The two causes differ, but they share one feature. Both say the workshop got information after 1583 that it lacked before, whether from voyages or from a Genoese chart. Both authors would accept that statement.

A.why: This is Text 1's inference, and it is the very claim Text 2 calls into question. You picked a statement only one author holds.

C.why: You assumed Text 2 attacks the observation. Text 2 opens by saying 'Morandi is right that the later charts are more accurate.' It disputes only why they improved, not whether they did.

D.why: You were drawn by Text 2's technical detail about erased outlines. Neither text says what those outlines show about survey methods, so neither author makes this claim.

stem: Based on the texts, both authors would most likely agree with which statement?
stimulus:
Text 1
Indigo-dyed linen fragments excavated at a medieval market town grow markedly paler in layers dated after 1350. Because the soil chemistry is uniform across all layers, textile historian Hana Okafor ruled out fading in the ground and concluded that rising indigo prices had led local dyers to use weaker dye baths.

Text 2
Okafor's color measurements are sound, but under scanning electron microscopy the later fibers show the abrasion and alkali pitting produced by repeated washing in lye soap, which became common in the town around 1350. Cloth dyed at full strength could have faded through laundering alone.
choices: Rising indigo prices after 1350 led local dyers to prepare weaker dye baths.
The color measurements exaggerate how much paler the later fragments are.
Lye soap became common in the town because indigo had grown too costly.
The later fragments had already become paler before they were buried.
explanation: Text 1 rules out fading in the ground and blames weaker dyeing, which happens before the cloth is ever used. Text 2 accepts the paleness and blames repeated laundering, which happens while the cloth is being worn. The two causes compete, but both act before burial. That shared timing is the one point both authors hold.

A.why: This is Okafor's conclusion. Text 2 argues that cloth dyed at full strength could have faded anyway, so it does not accept this claim.

B.why: You treated Text 2 as attacking the data. Text 2 calls Okafor's color measurements 'sound' and disputes only her explanation for them.

C.why: This joins a term from each text into a causal link that neither author makes. Neither text explains why lye soap spread.

stem: Based on the texts, both authors would most likely agree with which statement?
stimulus:
Text 1
Engineers embedded microcapsules of liquid monomer in a polymer, cracked the samples, and heated them to 80°C. The samples regained 90 percent of their original strength. The team concluded that heating had ruptured the capsules, releasing monomer that flowed into the cracks and bonded their faces.

Text 2
The recovery is well documented. Yet micro-CT scans of the same samples show that most capsules along the cracks remained intact. At 80°C, the polymer's own chains can soften and re-entangle across a crack face, so it is difficult to exclude heat alone as the cause of the healing.
choices: Heating the cracked samples played a part in their regaining strength.
The heat ruptured the capsules, releasing monomer that bonded the crack faces.
The samples regained considerably less strength than the engineers reported.
The microcapsules contributed nothing to the strength the samples regained.
explanation: In Text 1, heat triggers the capsules. In Text 2, heat makes the polymer chains re-entangle. The two texts disagree about the mechanism, but in both of them heating is part of how the samples recovered. That is the shared ground.

B.why: This is Text 1's mechanism. Text 2's scans show that most capsules stayed intact, which casts doubt on this claim.

C.why: Text 2 says outright that 'the recovery is well documented.' It accepts the result and questions only its cause.

D.why: You took Text 2 further than it goes. It says that most capsules, not all, stayed intact, and that heat alone is 'difficult to exclude.' It does not say the capsules did nothing, and Text 1 would reject this claim anyway.

stem: Based on the texts, both authors would most likely agree with which statement?
stimulus:
Text 1
Recording blackbirds in Vienna and in nearby forests, ornithologist Mira Ahn found that city birds' songs had a minimum frequency about 160 hertz higher. Since traffic noise is concentrated at low frequencies, Ahn concluded that urban blackbirds raise their pitch so that their songs are not masked.

Text 2
Reanalyzing Ahn's recordings with calibrated microphones, Teo Brandt found that the city songs were also considerably louder, as birds strain to be heard over traffic. In songbirds, singing louder raises pitch as a physical byproduct, so the higher frequencies may be an incidental consequence of volume rather than a shift to escape masking.
choices: City blackbirds raise their pitch in order to keep traffic noise from masking their songs.
The city recordings overstate how much higher urban songs are than forest songs.
Traffic noise is ultimately behind the higher pitch of the city blackbirds' songs.
City blackbirds sing more loudly because raising their pitch increases their volume.
explanation: Text 1 says that birds shift pitch to escape traffic noise. Text 2 says that birds sing louder to be heard over traffic, and the higher pitch follows as a byproduct. The paths differ, but in both accounts traffic noise is the root cause. The authors disagree only about whether the pitch change is a strategy or a side effect.

A.why: 'In order to' is Text 1's claim that the shift is deliberate. Text 2 calls the shift 'incidental,' so it rejects this statement.

B.why: Text 2 reanalyzes the same recordings and builds on the pitch difference without disputing it. It challenges the explanation, not the measurement.

D.why: This reverses Text 2's causal chain. In Text 2, loudness raises pitch, not the other way around.

stem: Based on the texts, both authors would most likely agree with which statement?
stimulus:
Text 1
After sea otters recolonized a stretch of the central California coast in 2016, divers recorded that purple sea urchin densities there fell by nearly 70 percent within two years. Ecologist Rosa Ibarra concluded that otter predation had driven the decline.

Text 2
Ibarra's survey counts are not in question. But when Jun Okada examined the empty urchin tests—the shells—that divers collected during those surveys, many bore the lesions of a wasting disease that swept the coast in 2017. Disease could have produced the same drop with or without otters.
choices: Otter predation was the main cause of the drop in urchin densities after 2016.
The divers' surveys overstated how sharply urchin densities fell after 2016.
The lesions on the collected urchin tests were left by otters attacking urchins.
The drop in urchin densities came from urchins dying rather than moving away.
explanation: Text 1's cause is predation and Text 2's is disease, and they compete. However, both are ways urchins die. Neither author suggests that the urchins left the site, so both would accept that the decline came from deaths.

A.why: This is Ibarra's inference. Text 2 says that disease could explain the same drop, so it does not grant this claim.

B.why: Text 2 begins by saying that the survey counts 'are not in question.' You chose an attack on the data when Text 2 attacks only the conclusion drawn from it.

C.why: You were drawn by the technical word 'lesions.' Text 2 attributes them to a wasting disease, and Text 1 never mentions them.

stem: Based on the texts, both authors would most likely agree with which statement?
stimulus:
Text 1
Commercial piano recordings made between 1905 and 1925 present Chopin's nocturnes at tempos as much as 20 percent faster than modern performances. Since the recordings' pitch confirms they are being played back at the correct speed, musicologist Ilse Varga concluded that pianists of the period simply preferred brisker tempos.

Text 2
Varga's measurements hold up, but a disc side then held barely four minutes of music. Comparing the same pianists' discs with their piano rolls, which had no such limit, Paolo Ruiz found consistently slower tempos on the rolls. Pianists may have hurried to fit a nocturne onto one side.
choices: The fast tempos on the discs reflect how quickly the pianists actually played.
Pianists of the period preferred brisker tempos than pianists do today.
The discs are played back too fast, which exaggerates the pianists' tempos.
Piano rolls preserve the period's tempos more faithfully than pitch analysis does.
explanation: Text 1 uses pitch to rule out a playback error and concludes that the pianists really played fast because they liked to. Text 2 accepts the measurements and says the pianists really played fast because they were short of time. Both agree that the speed is genuine and came from the pianists, not from the equipment. They differ only on why the pianists played that way.

B.why: This is Varga's conclusion. Ruiz's piano rolls show the same pianists playing slower when time was not limited, so Text 2 does not accept it.

C.why: Text 1 rules out a playback error by checking pitch, and Text 2 says that 'Varga's measurements hold up.' Neither author doubts the observation.

D.why: This sets two of the passage's technical terms against each other. Pitch analysis checks playback speed and is not a record of tempo, so the comparison answers a question neither text asks.

stem: Based on the texts, both authors would most likely agree with which statement?
stimulus:
Text 1
Twelve distance runners spent four weeks training at 2,400 meters, and afterward their 5,000-meter times at sea level improved by an average of 2 percent. Physiologist Dana Kerr attributed the gain to thin air stimulating the runners' bodies to produce more oxygen-carrying red blood cells.

Text 2
The runners did get faster. But carbon-monoxide rebreathing tests showed that half of them gained no measurable hemoglobin mass, yet they improved as much as the others. Since the camp also nearly doubled their weekly mileage, the extra training alone could account for the faster times.
choices: The thin air raised the runners' production of oxygen-carrying red blood cells.
The runners' faster times after the camp reflect timing errors, not real gains.
Something about the training camp was responsible for the runners' faster times.
Training at altitude has no effect on the hemoglobin mass of distance runners.
explanation: Text 1 credits the camp's altitude, and Text 2 credits the camp's extra mileage. Each points to a different feature of the same four weeks, but both treat the camp as the reason the runners improved. That is the claim they share.

A.why: This is Kerr's mechanism. Text 2 shows that half the runners gained no hemoglobin mass yet improved just as much, so it would not grant this as the explanation.

B.why: Text 2 opens with 'The runners did get faster.' You picked a challenge to the result when Text 2 challenges only its cause.

D.why: This stretches Text 2 into a universal claim. Text 2 reports that half of these twelve runners showed no gain, which implies the other half did, and Text 1 would reject the claim outright.

stem: Based on the texts, both authors would most likely agree with which statement?
stimulus:
Text 1
Of 64 versions of a Norwegian folktale collected in the 1890s, nearly every coastal version includes an episode in which the youngest son outwits a sea serpent; no inland version does. Folklorist Erik Haugen concluded that coastal storytellers had reshaped the tale around the hazards of their seafaring lives.

Text 2
Haugen's tally is accurate. Yet stylometric comparison shows that the coastal serpent episodes repeat, nearly phrase for phrase, a cheap chapbook that peddlers sold only in harbor towns in the 1870s. The episode may have entered through print, not through tellers' own invention.
choices: Coastal tellers invented the serpent episode to reflect the hazards of life at sea.
Something particular to coastal communities explains why their versions include the episode.
The collectors misrecorded the coastal versions, adding an episode the tellers omitted.
The chapbook's printer took the serpent episode from coastal storytellers' versions.
explanation: Text 1's explanation is seafaring life, which only coastal people had. Text 2's is a chapbook sold only in harbor towns, which only coastal people could buy. The sources compete, but each one reached the coast and not the inland villages. That is why both authors would accept this statement.

A.why: This is Haugen's inference. Text 2 suggests that the episode came from print, 'not through tellers' own invention,' so it does not grant this claim.

C.why: Text 2 calls Haugen's tally 'accurate.' It accepts that the episode appears in the coastal versions and questions only where it came from.

D.why: This reuses Text 2's chapbook but reverses its logic. Text 2 has the tellers borrowing from print, not the printer borrowing from them, and Text 1 never mentions a chapbook.
